issues.legal_issue: A contract may be in the course of a candidate’s trade or business even when that contract itself begins the business.
material_facts: The candidate held a subsisting mining lease, although he had not begun mining operations when he filed his nomination paper.
The lease was the transaction through which the candidate was to conduct the mining business.
issues.conclusion: The lease, if it was a contract, was in the course of the candidate’s business; earlier business transactions were not required.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 7(d) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, the contract must be entered into in the course of the candidate’s trade or business. A prior course of business based on other transactions is unnecessary; the contract in question may itself start the business. No earlier cases are relied on.

predicates.election_disqualification_proceeding: The proceeding challenges a candidate’s eligibility for election on the basis of a contract with the government.
predicates.contract_is_candidate_business_activity: The candidate entered into the contract as the activity through which the candidate would conduct a trade or business.

issues.definition: When an election-disqualification proceeding concerns a contract that is itself the candidate’s business activity, the contract is in the course of the candidate’s business.

issues.legal_issue: A government’s reserved right to pre-empt minerals does not, without an obligation to purchase or supply them, constitute a contract for the supply of goods.
material_facts: The mining lease reserved to the government a right, exercisable by written notice, to pre-empt minerals and their products.
The lessee was required to deliver minerals only after the government specified the quantity and time for supply in a notice.
The government was not required to pre-empt any minerals, and the lessee was not required to supply them unless the right was exercised.
issues.conclusion: The lease clause reserved a right of prior purchase but did not create a subsisting contract for the supply of goods.
issues.legal_principle: Section 7(d) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 requires a subsisting contract for the supply of goods to the appropriate government. A reservation of a right to purchase is not such a contract where the government has no obligation to buy and the candidate has no obligation to deliver unless a notice is served; a contract requires an offer and acceptance, not merely a reserved right. No earlier cases are relied on.

predicates.election_disqualification_proceeding: The proceeding challenges a candidate’s eligibility for election on the basis of a contract with the government.
predicates.government_has_only_preemption_right: The government has a reserved right to choose whether to purchase goods in preference to other purchasers.
predicates.no_purchase_or_supply_obligation_before_: Neither the government nor the candidate is obliged to buy or deliver the goods unless the government gives notice exercising its right.

issues.definition: In an election-disqualification proceeding, a government’s optional pre-emption right, without a purchase or supply obligation before notice, is not a contract for the supply of goods.

issues.legal_issue: A candidate is not disqualified on the ground of a government supply contract when a subsisting business contract contains only a right of pre-emption and creates no contract for the supply of goods.
material_facts: The candidate’s mining lease was subsisting and, if a contract, was in the course of his business.

The lease contained a right for the government to pre-empt minerals, but did not require the government to purchase any quantity or the candidate to supply minerals unless the government served notice.
The election challenge alleged disqualification under section 7(d) on the basis that the lease was a contract for the supply of goods.
issues.conclusion: The lease did not disqualify the candidate under section 7(d); the appeal was dismissed and the decision reversing the election tribunal was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: Section 7(d) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 requires a subsisting contract entered into in the course of the candidate’s trade or business with the appropriate government for the supply of goods or execution of works. Although the lease was subsisting and in the course of business, its pre-emption clause did not create a contract for supply. No earlier cases are relied on.

rule.if: election_disqualification_proceeding and subsisting_candidate_business_contract and government_has_only_preemption_right and no_purchase_or_supply_obligation_before_notice

predicates.election_disqualification_proceeding: The proceeding challenges a candidate’s election eligibility on the ground that a government contract disqualifies the candidate.
predicates.subsisting_candidate_business_contract: A contract between the candidate and the government remains in existence and was entered into as part of the candidate’s business.
predicates.government_has_only_preemption_right: The government has a reserved right to choose whether to purchase goods in preference to other purchasers.
predicates.no_purchase_or_supply_obligation_before_: Neither the government nor the candidate is obliged to buy or deliver the goods unless the government gives notice exercising its right.

issues.definition: A candidate with a subsisting business contract is not disqualified on the supply-contract ground when the government holds only an optional pre-emption right and neither party has a purchase or supply obligation before notice.
